## Describe a plan[#](https://sourdough.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/describe-a-plan.html#describe-a-plan)

Instead of choosing flags, describe what the app does in a sentence and let an OpenAI-compatible model plan it. This page covers the command, the model configuration, the plan format, and the steps a plan becomes; when you have a plan you trust, save it to a file and generate with `--plan`.

### Describe it in a sentence[#](https://sourdough.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/describe-a-plan.html#describe-it-in-a-sentence)

```bash
sourdough new --describe "A blog with posts and comments"
```

Sourdough asks an OpenAI-compatible model for a plan, validates it against `resources/plan.schema.json`, and prints it. The model kneads the dough, but you decide when the loaf is ready to bake: if the answer is not valid JSON, does not match the schema, or the model gives up after one retry, Sourdough refuses with a message pointing you to `--plan=<file>` (exit `1`). You write the plan yourself and pass it in.

The model does the work but never gates. When an answer fails, Sourdough retries once, telling the model why the previous answer was not valid. If the second answer fails too, the command stops with:

```text
The model could not produce a valid plan. Write the plan yourself and pass it with --plan=<file>.
```

### See the plan without writing anything[#](https://sourdough.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/describe-a-plan.html#see-the-plan-without-writing-anything)

```bash
sourdough new --describe "A blog with posts and comments" --plan-only
```

### Pass a ready-made plan[#](https://sourdough.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/describe-a-plan.html#pass-a-ready-made-plan)

`--describe` stops at the plan: baking straight from a description is not built yet. Save the plan to a file and pass it with `--plan`, which bakes it:

```bash
sourdough new my-app --plan plan.json
```

`--plan` reads the file, validates it against the schema, and continues the normal generation flow using the plan's permutation and name. A file ending in `.yaml` or `.yml` is read as YAML, anything else as JSON. A missing file, or a file that does not parse or does not match the schema, is refused with the reason printed.

### The plan stays with the app[#](https://sourdough.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/describe-a-plan.html#the-plan-stays-with-the-app)

The bake saves the plan in the app as `.sourdough/plan.yaml`, next to the manifest, so the app keeps a record of what it was asked to be. It is a valid plan file, so the same loaf bakes again from it:

```bash
sourdough new my-app-copy --plan my-app/.sourdough/plan.yaml
```

Sourdough never rewrites it after the bake: `sourdough feed` and `sourdough manifest --check` leave it alone, and you may edit it as the app grows. Commit it with the manifest. See [The saved plan](https://sourdough.apps.wayne.edu/docs/reference/plan-format.html#the-saved-plan).

### Model configuration[#](https://sourdough.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/describe-a-plan.html#model-configuration)

`--describe` needs three environment variables (no defaults, no key in code):

| Variable | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `SOURDOUGH_LLM_BASE_URL` | the OpenAI-compatible endpoint, including the API path (usually `/v1`) |
| `SOURDOUGH_LLM_API_KEY` | the API key |
| `SOURDOUGH_LLM_MODEL` | the model name |

Any OpenAI-compatible endpoint works: a hosted API, a local server, or WarriorGPT. Sourdough does not care about the hostname; it only needs the base URL, key, and model.

Warning

`SOURDOUGH_LLM_API_KEY` is a credential. Set it in your environment and keep it out of the repository; Sourdough reads it from the environment and keeps no key in code.

If a variable is missing, the command names it and points you at the alternative:

```text
The SOURDOUGH_LLM_MODEL environment variable is not set. Set it, or pass a ready-made plan with --plan=<file>.
```

### What a plan looks like[#](https://sourdough.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/describe-a-plan.html#what-a-plan-looks-like)

A plan is a small JSON object:

```json
{
    "permutation": "raw",
    "parts": ["sesame", "helmet"],
    "name": "my-app",
    "models": [
        {
            "name": "Post",
            "fields": [
                { "name": "title", "type": "string" },
                { "name": "body", "type": "text" }
            ]
        }
    ],
    "pages": ["/", "/posts"]
}
```

`permutation`, `parts`, and `name` are required; `models` and `pages` are optional. `parts` is a subset of `sesame`, `helmet`, `proctor`, and `preflight`.

### The steps a plan produces[#](https://sourdough.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/describe-a-plan.html#the-steps-a-plan-produces)

The plan becomes a list of plain steps, built from the permutation, the target dir, the local runtime flags (`--sail` and `--docker`) and whether ADVISOR is wired in (`--no-advisor` opts out). For the raw shape the steps are:

- `Copy the raw template into <dir>`
- `Replace {{app_name}} and {{app_slug}} in file names and contents`

The raw + Vue shape starts with `Copy the raw template, then the raw-vue template over it, into <dir>` and the same replace step. The Laravel shapes get one step to create the app in the target dir. Permutations that keep ADVISOR get `Wire ADVISOR into the app`; `--sail` adds `Use Sail for the local runtime (compose.yaml, laravel/sail in require-dev)` and `--docker` adds `Use Docker for the local runtime (Dockerfile, compose.yaml, MySQL 8.4)`. The two flags are mutually exclusive: together they are refused with `Choose one of --sail or --docker, not both.`

Note

`--sail` and `--docker` are for the Laravel paths: the raw paths run on plain PHP. Combining them with a raw permutation is refused.

In 0.1 all five permutations are generated.

### Related[#](https://sourdough.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/describe-a-plan.html#related)

- [Pick a shape](https://sourdough.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/shapes.html)
- [The manifest](https://sourdough.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/manifest.html)

Source: https://sourdough.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/every-os.html

## Every developer, every operating system[#](https://sourdough.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/every-os.html#every-developer-every-operating-system)

Sourdough is one PHP command, so it works on Windows, macOS, and Linux: the same `sourdough new` invocation, the same flags, the same output, no matter which OS you sit at. This page covers why that holds and the practices that keep generated apps portable across all three systems. If you are baking an app, start with [Quick start](https://sourdough.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/quick-start.html) and come back here when a coworker on another OS hits a snag.

### One PHP command, three operating systems[#](https://sourdough.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/every-os.html#one-php-command-three-operating-systems)

Because the CLI is a single PHP command, there is no per-OS build and no shell dependency in the happy path. Developer scripts follow the same rule: a script that developers run ships as a `.ps1` and a `.sh` that do the same thing, or is one PHP command. Prefer the single PHP command when the logic is more than a few lines. Windows never needs bash or WSL to run the CLI.

### Line endings travel with the repo[#](https://sourdough.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/every-os.html#line-endings-travel-with-the-repo)

Every generated app ships a `.gitattributes` with `* text=auto eol=lf`, and sets `.ps1`, `.bat` and `.cmd` to CRLF. The file travels with the repo and gives every contributor the same rules, which beats the per-user `core.autocrlf` setting. Anything that runs on Citadel must be LF, so the checks fail when `build.sh`, release scripts or `deployments/*` contain CRLF, and when two paths differ only by case: macOS and Windows ignore case and Citadel does not, so an app can work on every laptop and break on deploy.

### Native paths for each OS[#](https://sourdough.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/every-os.html#native-paths-for-each-os)

Windows gets PowerShell (`.ps1`), which never needs bash or WSL. Linux and macOS get bash (`.sh`), written for macOS's stock bash 3.2 and BSD tools. Be aware that PowerShell's default policy on Windows clients can block scripts that were downloaded from the internet (Microsoft calls the policy defense in depth, not a security boundary). Scripts the generator writes locally are not affected, but the docs should say what to do if a script is blocked. Laravel's own install page gives Windows users `Set-ExecutionPolicy Bypass -Scope Process -Force` followed by downloading a script and passing it to `iex`; that is a pattern WSU docs should not copy.

### Subprocesses as argument arrays[#](https://sourdough.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/every-os.html#subprocesses-as-argument-arrays)

Whenever Sourdough runs Composer, npm, git or Docker, it passes the command as an array of arguments, never as a shell string. That accepts paths with spaces and Windows drive letters, keeps quoting differences between PowerShell and bash out of the picture, and skips shell parsing of a directory name on Linux and macOS. Set timeouts on every subprocess.

Windows has a catch. When the target is a `.bat` or `.cmd` file, Windows starts `cmd.exe`, which splits arguments by its own rules, and callers must escape for it; Composer and npm are usually `.bat` or `.cmd` shims on Windows. PHP's array form of `proc_open` had a command injection on Windows, and its first fix was incomplete; the fixes are in PHP 8.1.29, 8.2.20 and 8.3.8, and the stack's PHP floor already rules out the unpatched builds. So: keep the array form; where you can, run `php.exe` with `composer.phar` and `node.exe` with npm's JavaScript entry point instead of the shims; never pass user-chosen text (an app name, a path) to a shim; and validate names before they reach a command line.

### More than one local runtime[#](https://sourdough.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/every-os.html#more-than-one-local-runtime)

Offer more than one local runtime, and be honest about Sail on Windows. Sail is Laravel's Docker development environment; on Windows it needs WSL2 and its `sail` script is shell. Docker's own advice for WSL2 is to keep source code inside the Linux file system, because bind mounts from the Windows side are slower and do not deliver file-change events. So the routes are: Docker Compose with a Citadel-parity image as the route that works natively on every OS, Sail as an option where it fits, and plain PHP with Composer. Laravel's docs also offer Herd, a native macOS and Windows environment with PHP, Nginx, Node and the `laravel` CLI.

Note

Treat Sail as a development tool. Its compose file and images are for local work; do not reuse them as the production image, because they carry dev tools, ports and defaults that a production container should not.

### Docker images the safe way[#](https://sourdough.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/every-os.html#docker-images-the-safe-way)

If Sourdough generates a Dockerfile: pin the base image to an exact version (a digest is stronger), use a multi-stage build, run as a non-root user with a fixed UID, add a `.dockerignore`, never leave secrets in a layer, and rebuild regularly with `--pull`. State the CPU architecture: the base images behind `--docker` are pinned by manifest-list digest, so one pin resolves natively on amd64 and arm64 and Apple Silicon users do not run under emulation. Pinning to a digest also opts you out of automatic security fixes, so pair the pin with a scheduled update.

### Test on all three systems[#](https://sourdough.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/every-os.html#test-on-all-three-systems)

Run the generator and the generated app's tests on Windows, macOS and Linux, or run a written smoke test before each minor release. Path, newline and shell bugs only appear on the system you did not test.

### Templates as archives[#](https://sourdough.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/every-os.html#templates-as-archives)

Fetch templates as Composer dist archives, not with `git clone --recurse-submodules`. A carriage return in a submodule path turned into code execution during a recursive clone in a Git vulnerability, fixed across many releases and listed as exploited by CISA. Name the Git floor for developers and keep Git current. Composer 2.10 no longer falls back from dist to source by default, which helps here.

### Related[#](https://sourdough.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/every-os.html#related)

- [Pick a shape](https://sourdough.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/shapes.html)
- [Building on Laravel](https://sourdough.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/laravel.html)
- [Testing](https://sourdough.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/testing.html)
- [CI](https://sourdough.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/ci.html)

Source: https://sourdough.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/keeping-current.html

## Keeping apps current[#](https://sourdough.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/keeping-current.html#keeping-apps-current)

A project that was fresh on the day it was generated is stale a month later, so this page is about keeping generated apps fed: what the manifest records, how `sourdough feed` merges template updates in without clobbering your changes, and how CI tells you when an app falls behind. Like any starter, it needs regular feeding, or it goes flat. Commit the manifest in your app, keep the `sourdough-feed` job every shape's pipeline ships with, then read on.

### Record where the app came from[#](https://sourdough.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/keeping-current.html#record-where-the-app-came-from)

Every app carries a `.sourdough/manifest.json` recording the Sourdough version, the template, the answers you chose, and a sha256 hash of every file, each marked `managed` or `seeded`. Other tools do the same: Copier writes `.copier-answers.yml`, and cruft writes `.cruft.json`. Without this record there is nothing to compare against, so no update is possible.

Warning

Do not hand-edit the manifest. It is the starter's memory: it remembers what went into the loaf, so `feed` knows what to refresh and what to leave to rise on its own.

[The manifest](https://sourdough.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/manifest.html) has the full key list and the managed/seeded split.

### Check for drift[#](https://sourdough.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/keeping-current.html#check-for-drift)

`sourdough manifest --check` lists the managed files that have drifted from the manifest, the ones you (or someone) edited since Sourdough wrote them:

```bash
sourdough manifest --check
```

Exit codes: `0` clean, `1` a managed file changed or is missing, `2` tool error (no manifest, or no `--check`). Seeded files are never reported. They're yours. Line endings are forgiven, as `feed` forgives them: a checkout that turned a file to CRLF (the raw shapes' `.gitattributes` does it for `*.ps1`) has not drifted. Drift is not wrong: `feed` merges your edits with the template's. The check tells you which files a feed will have to merge rather than simply replace, which is why the [CI job](https://sourdough.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/keeping-current.html#feed-in-ci) reports drift and never fails on it.

### Feed the app: a merge, not an overwrite[#](https://sourdough.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/keeping-current.html#feed-the-app-a-merge-not-an-overwrite)

Upgrade the Sourdough CLI first ([Upgrading](https://sourdough.apps.wayne.edu/docs/upgrading.html)), then, in the app, on a clean git tree, look before you leap:

```bash
sourdough feed --dry-run
```

The plan lists one line per file that would change, with the reason, and writes nothing:

```
Would feed the laravel-inertia app: Sourdough 0.1.5 to 0.1.6 (dry run: nothing written)
  update    config/helmet.php (you had not changed it)
  merge     routes/web.php (your edits kept, the template's merged in)
  conflict  vite.config.ts (1 conflicting hunk: you and the template changed the same lines; resolve the markers)
Would keep the template's version of 2 changed files in .sourdough/base/, so the next feed can merge from it.
Plan: 1 update, 1 merge, 1 conflict.
```

Then feed it for real, and review it like any other change:

```bash
sourdough feed
git status
git diff
```

#### What feed does[#](https://sourdough.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/keeping-current.html#what-feed-does)

Feed is the update model of Copier and cruft (ADR-0014), built on plain git instead of a Python runtime:

1. It reads `.sourdough/manifest.json`: the template, your answers, and a sha256 of every file Sourdough wrote last time (the base).
2. It bakes the same shape with the same answers, with the Sourdough you have installed, into a scratch folder: the loaf `sourdough new` would bake today. `new` and `feed` bake through the same code, so the two cannot disagree.
3. It compares the three versions of each file (the base, your app's, the new loaf's) and acts:

| The template | Your app | Feed |
| --- | --- | --- |
| did not change it | anything | leaves it alone (no line in the plan) |
| changed it | never touched it | `update`: takes the template's new version |
| changed it | changed it too | `merge`: `git merge-file` applies the template's change on top of yours |
| changed it | already has the new version | `record`: nothing written; the manifest records the new version |
| changed the same lines | changed them too | `conflict`: git's markers in the file, `<<<<<<< app` ... `>>>>>>> sourdough <version>` |
| added it | has no such file | `add` |
| added it | has the very same file | `record`: nothing written; the manifest takes the file in |
| added it | has its own file there | `conflict`: both versions marked |
| dropped it | never touched it | `remove` (and its emptied folder) |
| dropped it | changed it | `keep`: it is yours now, and leaves the manifest |
| changed it | deleted it | `keep`: it stays deleted |

A `record` line changes no file, only the manifest, so `sourdough manifest --check` stops calling the file changed. It is how an app baked by Sourdough 0.1.6 with `--sail` or `--docker` catches up: 0.1.6 wrote the manifest before the oven's scaffold ran, so feed reads the oven from the app's files (it says so in a `note:` line) and records them.

Seeded files (`README.md`, `.env.example`, `package-lock.json`) are never touched; a seeded file new to the template is written only where you have none. A feed that changes `package.json` leaves your lock file alone, so run `npm install` and commit both files, or the pipeline's `npm ci` stops on the mismatch. Line endings are forgiven: a Windows checkout with CRLF endings still matches what Sourdough wrote, and the files feed writes keep your checkout's endings. Binary files are never merged: the template's copy lands next to yours as `<file>.sourdough-new`.

4. It moves the manifest to the new base (the new loaf's hashes and the new Sourdough version) and keeps the template's version of every managed file you have changed in `.sourdough/base/<file>.base`. Commit both.

#### Where the base comes from[#](https://sourdough.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/keeping-current.html#where-the-base-comes-from)

A three-way merge needs the version Sourdough wrote last time. The manifest records only its hash, so feed finds the content by that hash: first in `.sourdough/base/` (kept by the previous feed), then in any commit of your app's git history (the commit right after `sourdough new` holds every file as baked). A candidate is used only when its sha256 matches the manifest, so a wrong base can never sneak in.

When neither has it (you edited a file before your first commit), feed cannot tell your edits from the template's, so it does not guess: every place the two versions differ is marked as a conflict, and the lines they share stand once. Commit right after `sourdough new` and this never happens.

#### Conflicts[#](https://sourdough.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/keeping-current.html#conflicts)

A conflict is never a silent overwrite. Feed exits `1`, and the file holds git's markers:

```
<<<<<<< app
your version
=======
the template's version
>>>>>>> sourdough 0.1.6
```

Edit the file to what it should be, delete the markers, and run your checks. `git diff --check` lists any markers left behind, so put it in a pre-commit hook or CI. Until the markers (and any `.sourdough-new` copies) are gone, the next feed refuses with exit `2` and lists them: finish one feeding before the next.

#### Rules feed keeps[#](https://sourdough.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/keeping-current.html#rules-feed-keeps)

- **A clean git tree first.** Copier recommends a clean `git status` but does not enforce it; feed enforces it (exit `2`), untracked files included, so `git status` and `git diff` show exactly what it did. To undo a whole feed: `git restore . && git clean -fd`.
- **Git, and only git.** Feed needs git on PATH (or `SOURDOUGH_GIT` pointing at it), on Windows, macOS and Linux alike. The Laravel shapes also bake on a fresh `laravel/laravel` skeleton through Composer, the same as `sourdough new`, so feeding one needs Composer and the network; Laravel's own skeleton updates arrive as template updates, merged the same way.
- **Forward only.** A manifest written by a newer Sourdough than the one running is refused (exit `2`). Update Sourdough first: a starter only rises forward.
- **The answers stay.** Feed bakes with the answers in the manifest (the shape, `--sail` or `--docker`, Playbook and ADVISOR). It does not change them.
- **The plan is yours.** `.sourdough/plan.yaml`, the plan the app was baked from, is not in the manifest: feed never reads, rewrites or removes it, and never lists it in its plan, so editing it is not drift. An app baked before Sourdough saved its plan gets none written by feed. See [The saved plan](https://sourdough.apps.wayne.edu/docs/reference/plan-format.html#the-saved-plan).

#### Exit codes[#](https://sourdough.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/keeping-current.html#exit-codes)

| Run | `0` | `1` | `2` |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `sourdough feed` | fed cleanly, or nothing to feed | fed, with conflicts to resolve | tool error: no manifest, no git, a dirty tree, conflicts left from the last feed, a newer manifest, a failed bake |
| `sourdough feed --dry-run` | fresh: nothing to feed | feeding would change files | tool error |

Add `--json` to either for a machine-readable plan: the template, `from` and `to` versions, one entry per file (`path`, `action`, `detail`), a summary count per action, the base copies, any notes, and the exit code.

#### Feed in CI[#](https://sourdough.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/keeping-current.html#feed-in-ci)

Every shape's `.gitlab-ci.yml` ships a `sourdough-feed` job, so an app that falls behind its template says so in its own pipeline instead of surfacing as drift months later; that is what makes a starter "fed". The job runs on the shape's `composer` image (multi-arch, through `${IMAGE_PREFIX}`, on the `.composer-cache`), installs the newest Sourdough release with `composer create-project`, and asks it two questions:

```yaml
sourdough-feed:
  extends: .composer-cache
  image: ${IMAGE_PREFIX}/composer:2.10.3
  variables:
    SOURDOUGH_HOME: /tmp/sourdough
  allow_failure:
    exit_codes: [1]
  script:
    - composer create-project --no-dev --no-interaction --no-progress --prefer-dist waynestate/sourdough "$SOURDOUGH_HOME"
    - mkdir -p .git/info && echo .cache/ >> .git/info/exclude
    - drift=0; php "$SOURDOUGH_HOME/bin/sourdough" manifest --check || drift=$?
    - fed=0; php "$SOURDOUGH_HOME/bin/sourdough" feed --dry-run || fed=$?
    - if [ "$drift" -gt 1 ] || [ "$fed" -gt 1 ]; then exit 2; fi
    - if [ "$fed" -eq 1 ]; then echo "This app has template changes to feed. Run sourdough feed, review and commit." >&2; exit 1; fi
```

What each answer does to the pipeline, read from the commands' own exit codes:

| The app | `manifest --check` | `feed --dry-run` | The job |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| fresh, as baked or fed | `0` clean | `0` fresh | passes |
| a managed file edited by hand | `1`, one `changed` line per file | `0` fresh | passes, with the files listed: drift is normal, and feed merges it |
| a newer release has template changes it has not fed | `0` or `1` | `1`, the plan | warns: exit `1`, which `allow_failure` shows as a warning, so a pending feed never blocks a deploy |
| a broken record: no manifest, one from a newer Sourdough, conflicts left over from the last feed, a failed bake | `2` | `2` | fails |

To clear the warning, feed the app on your machine (upgrade the CLI, `sourdough feed`, review, commit); the next pipeline is green again. The `.git/info/exclude` line keeps the restored `.cache/` download folder out of git's view, so the dry run sees the clean tree a real feed needs. `tests/TemplateFeedJobTest.php` holds every shape to the same job and runs its lines on a fresh bake of each shape: clean, edited, behind and broken.

Copier's `copier check-update` is the same idea: `--quiet` makes it exit 2 when an update exists, and `--output-format json` gives machines the answer.

#### Apps Sourdough did not make, and WELD[#](https://sourdough.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/keeping-current.html#apps-sourdough-did-not-make-and-weld)

Feed needs the manifest `sourdough new` writes. An app without one (an app Sourdough did not make, or WELD itself, which was built by hand and checks its drift against a fresh Inertia bake with its own regen check) gets exit `2`. Writing a manifest into an existing app is `sourdough adopt`'s job (ADR-0014), which is not built yet.

### Versioned template releases[#](https://sourdough.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/keeping-current.html#versioned-template-releases)

Tag template releases with semantic versions, and put a short "what changed, what to do" entry in the changelog for each. Copier picks the newest tag by default. An update tool is only as good as the history it can read.

### Compatibility CI[#](https://sourdough.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/keeping-current.html#compatibility-ci)

On every change to Sourdough, and on every release of WayneUI, SESAME, HELMET and PROCTOR, generate each permutation, install it and run its own tests and the PROCTOR check. Run it on a schedule (nightly), not only on changes, covering PHP 8.4 and 8.5 and the current and previous Laravel major. The starter is the place where all the stack libraries meet, so it is where a break shows first. A starter with no commits still rots, because the things it depends on keep moving.

### Keep templates thin[#](https://sourdough.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/keeping-current.html#keep-templates-thin)

Put shared behavior in libraries, not in the template. Code that lives in SESAME, HELMET and PROCTOR updates with `composer update`, so only the glue lives in the template and the merge stays small. Other universities ship starters the same way: a Composer package plus an install command. A new site installs it with `composer require` and `php artisan starterkit:install`, and an existing site can require the library without publishing the project files. This is the core-plus-adapters rule applied to the starter itself.

### Owners, windows and sunsets[#](https://sourdough.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/keeping-current.html#owners-windows-and-sunsets)

Starters die quietly. The React team deprecated Create React App on 2025-02-14, saying it had no active maintainers, and installing it now prints a warning that points at current frameworks. Laravel replaced Breeze and Jetstream with new kits when Laravel 12 shipped. Each permutation should name an owner, tie its support window to the framework and PHP end dates, run the scheduled build, and have the check print a deprecation notice with the migration note.

### Refreshing the Squire templates[#](https://sourdough.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/keeping-current.html#refreshing-the-squire-templates)

The deploy files in your app (`build.sh`, `scripts/release.sh`, the `.squire/` config, and their friends) come from Squire's exported copy, checked into the Sourdough repository at `templates/squire/`. Squire owns them; Sourdough installs them as-is and records them in the manifest, so you never edit them by hand. When Squire's templates change, regenerate the copy from a Squire checkout, then verify it:

```bash
php ../squire/bin/export-templates.php --to=../sourdough/templates/squire
php ../squire/bin/export-templates.php --to=../sourdough/templates/squire --check
```

Commit the refreshed copy with the Squire commit in the message, and add a CHANGELOG line. From the installed package the same refresh is `composer squire-copy:sync`, verified by `composer squire-copy:check` (part of `composer ci`). Apps generated earlier pick up the refreshed files with their next `sourdough feed`.

- [The manifest](https://sourdough.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/manifest.html)

## Building on Laravel[#](https://sourdough.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/laravel.html#building-on-laravel)

This page covers what a Laravel bake adds over the raw base and the practices that keep Laravel shapes sound. Start by picking your shape on [Pick a shape](https://sourdough.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/shapes.html), then come back here for what the bake gives you and how to keep it healthy.

A Laravel loaf bakes from a fresh Laravel skeleton, not from the raw base: `sourdough new --laravel` starts from Composer's official installer and layers the stack on top, so the app inherits Laravel's upgrades to the skeleton.

### What a Laravel bake adds[#](https://sourdough.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/laravel.html#what-a-laravel-bake-adds)

- `--laravel` bakes a Laravel + Blade app: a fresh Laravel skeleton from Composer, the laravel-blade overlay, the stack packages, Squire's laravel deploy files and the manifest.
- `--laravel --vue` bakes a Laravel + Blade + Vue islands app: the Laravel + Blade bake under a front-end layer (Vite with the Vue plugin, a `resources/js/app.js` registry that mounts a Vue 3 app on every `[data-vue-island]` element, and a Counter island live on the dashboard view).
- `--inertia` bakes a Laravel + Inertia/Vue app: the same Laravel skeleton, the laravel-inertia overlay (Inertia 3 pages rendered by Vue and drawn by WayneUI: its app bar, sidebar, drawer, footer and components from `@waynestate/wayne-ui-css` and `@waynestate/wayne-ui-vue` 2.0.8, pinned exactly; no Tailwind; ESLint bans the old kit's `components/ui` imports; Ziggy routes; the stack packages; a `frontend` CI job that lints, type-checks and builds), Squire's laravel deploy files and the manifest.

All three Laravel shapes also ship Laravel Boost as a dev-only tool, with the stack's guidelines and starter rules in `.ai/` (see [Laravel Boost, dev only](https://sourdough.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/laravel.html#laravel-boost-dev-only)).

All five permutations bake; the raw ones (`--raw`, `--raw --vue`) start from the raw base instead of a Laravel skeleton.

### Build on the official installer[#](https://sourdough.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/laravel.html#build-on-the-official-installer)

For Laravel paths, wrap the supported entry points instead of copying Laravel's skeleton by hand. `composer create-project laravel/laravel` picks the newest major, which is right. The installer also accepts a community starter kit published on Packagist:

```bash
laravel new my-app --using=vendor/kit
```

A kit declares its environment variables in `.env.example` and its setup steps in the `post-create-project-cmd` list of its `composer.json`. There is no plain Blade kit, so the `--laravel` (Blade) and Blade-plus-Vue-islands permutations are a bare Laravel install plus Sourdough's own layer, not a vendor kit.

### Local runtime: Sail or Docker[#](https://sourdough.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/laravel.html#local-runtime-sail-or-docker)

The Laravel paths take a flag for the local runtime, and the two are mutually exclusive: together they are refused with `Choose one of --sail or --docker, not both.`

- `--sail` runs the app on Laravel Sail. The bake adds `laravel/sail` to require-dev, writes a `compose.yaml`, sets the database settings in `.env.example` and appends a "Run it locally with Sail" README section. The database is MySQL 8.4 LTS. Sail serves as its own `sail` user, so when the checkout is one that user cannot write (a Windows drive, or files a root container wrote), the compose file opens the app's files to it before Sail starts (`vendor/`, `node_modules/` and `.git` are left alone). Without that, every page was a 500 naming `tempnam()`. On a normal Linux or macOS checkout nothing changes.
- `--docker` writes the app's own Docker setup after the shape is baked: a two-target `Dockerfile` (dev and prod) whose base images are pinned by manifest-list digest, a `compose.yaml` with a MySQL 8.4 service (and a vite service for the Vue and Inertia shapes, which runs `npm install` on its first start and then `npm run dev` with `LARAVEL_SAIL=1` so `public/hot` says `http://localhost:5173`, an address your browser can load), a `.dockerignore`, the PHP ini files the image copies in, the `composer dev-up`, `dev-down` and `dev-shell` scripts, the database settings in `.env.example`, and a "Run it locally with Docker" README section. It works natively on Windows, macOS and Linux (no WSL2 needed) and is checked on amd64 and arm64.

Sail is Laravel's Docker development environment. On Windows it needs WSL2 and its `sail` script is shell, so it is an option where it fits, never the only Windows route; `--docker` is the route that works natively. See [Every developer, every operating system](https://sourdough.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/every-os.html) for the full picture.

With `--docker`, the production build takes Playbook's credentials as a BuildKit secret, never a build arg:

```bash
docker build --target prod --secret id=composer_auth,src=auth.json -t myapp .
```

The `FROM` lines in the generated `Dockerfile` are the single place to swap in Squire's Citadel-parity image when it exists.

### Sign-in stays SESAME[#](https://sourdough.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/laravel.html#sign-in-stays-sesame)

Laravel's kits ship registration, password reset, email verification and two-factor login through Fortify. A WSU app signs in through SESAME, so turn off the features you do not use, and remove their routes from the front end too. In the Vue, React and Svelte kits a leftover reference to a disabled route breaks the build, because routes are generated at build time.

Warning

A live `/register` route in an app that is supposed to use central sign-in is a security hole and a support burden. The kits also set a login rate limit (5 a minute per email and IP in the docs' example), and the WorkOS variants would add a second hosted identity provider beside SESAME, so leave them out.

### Laravel Boost, dev only[#](https://sourdough.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/laravel.html#laravel-boost-dev-only)

Every Laravel bake (Blade, Blade with Vue, Inertia) ships [Laravel Boost](https://laravel.com/docs/boost) in `require-dev`: an MCP server, guidelines and skills that teach a coding agent the app's Laravel. Boost is used as published, through its own commands and file layout. Sourdough adds the stack's guidance and the guard rails around it. [ADVISOR](https://github.com/waynestate/advisor) complements Boost, never replaces it: Boost knows Laravel, ADVISOR knows the Wayne State stack.

After `composer install`, each developer wires Boost into their own agent once per checkout:

```bash
php artisan boost:install
```

What the bake gives you:

| Piece | Where | In git? |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Boost itself | `laravel/boost ^2.10` in `require-dev` | yes (`composer.json`) |
| The stack's conventions (SESAME, WayneUI, HELMET, MySQL 5.6, Oracle, Squire) | `.ai/guidelines/wayne-state.md`, folded into every agent's file by Boost | yes, managed: `sourdough feed` refreshes it |
| Starter project rules | `.ai/rules/migrations.md`, `.ai/rules/routes.md` and Boost's `.ai/rules/index.md` | yes, seeded: the team's from the first commit |
| What `boost:install` writes | `CLAUDE.md`, `AGENTS.md`, `.mcp.json`, `.claude/skills/`, `.junie/`, `boost.json` | no: a `.gitignore` block keeps them out |
| A refresh after `composer update` | `composer boost-update`, appended to Laravel's `post-update-cmd` | yes |
| A check that Boost stays a dev tool | `tests/Feature/BoostDevOnlyTest.php` | yes |

Why each choice:

- **`boost.json` is ignored.** It records the agents each developer picked, so it is personal. Boost's docs allow ignoring it.
- **The refresh is guarded.** Boost's docs suggest `@php artisan boost:update --ansi` in `post-update-cmd`, but `boost:update` exits 1 until `boost:install` has written `boost.json`, and under `composer update --no-dev` the command does not exist. `composer boost-update` runs it only when `vendor/laravel/boost` is installed and `boost.json` names at least one agent (Boost's own precondition; a `boost:install` that found no agent leaves an empty list), and passes its exit code through, so a real failure still fails `composer update`.
- **The agent files are ignored whole.** Git cannot ignore the generated block inside `CLAUDE.md`, and Boost rewrites that block on every `boost:update`. Team guidance goes in `.ai/guidelines/`, which Boost folds into every agent's file, so nothing is lost.
- **The skeleton's `CLAUDE.md` and `AGENTS.md` are dropped.** Laravel 13 ships them holding only a bootstrap block that tells an agent to `composer require laravel/boost --dev` (already done) and to install PHP with a remote PowerShell one-liner the stack does not copy. `boost:install` writes them again for the agents you pick. A skeleton file with anything else in it is kept.
- **`.agents/` stays tracked.** Booster keeps its playbooks in `.agents/skills/`, and Boost writes its Codex, OpenCode, Amp and Antigravity skills there too, so commit what you want to keep from that folder.
- **Record rules through your agent.** Ask it to "remember" something and Boost's `record-rule` tool files it in `.ai/rules/` and rewrites the index; a rule file added by hand is not found until `php artisan boost:index-rules` runs.

Boost never reaches production. Squire's `scripts/release.sh` and the `--docker` prod target both install with `composer install --no-dev`, which leaves `require-dev` behind, and `BoostDevOnlyTest` fails when `laravel/boost` moves into `require` or the lock file puts it outside `packages-dev`. Boost 2.10 needs PHP 8.2 or newer and Laravel 11.45, 12.41 or 13.

Warning

Boost's MCP server can run database queries and code through Tinker, so the development `.env` must point at a local database and never at the shared server.

### Support windows[#](https://sourdough.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/laravel.html#support-windows)

Laravel gives each major 18 months of bug fixes and two years of security fixes. From its release notes: 11 reached the end of security fixes on 2026-03-12; 12 (PHP 8.2 to 8.5) gets security fixes until 2027-02-24; 13 (PHP 8.3 to 8.5) until 2028-03-17. Name the major in the generator's tests, so a new release cannot change output unseen, and print the end-of-security date in the generated README. Laravel 13 needs PHP 8.3, which is also the stack's floor: 8.2 security support ends 2026-12-31.

### Trust the HA-Proxy, not every sender[#](https://sourdough.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/laravel.html#trust-the-ha-proxy-not-every-sender)

Citadel ends TLS at HA-Proxy, so the app sees plain HTTP. Behind a balancer that ends TLS, Laravel's `url` helper can produce `http` links until `trustProxies` is set in `bootstrap/app.php`. The generated app should list the proxy addresses (from env) and also set `trustHosts`. Raw PHP gets the same behavior from HELMET.

### /up for liveness, /ready for traffic[#](https://sourdough.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/laravel.html#up-for-liveness-ready-for-traffic)

`/up` is Laravel's health route and the liveness answer: 200 whenever the app boots, and it never looks at the database or the cache, so a database blip cannot restart every container at once. `/ready` asks the other question, "should this instance get traffic right now?". Every Laravel shape registers HELMET's readiness route there, in `bootstrap/app.php` (the `then:` callback, outside the web group, so a probe writes no session row and sets no cookie), with three app checks next to HELMET's own:

| Check | Class | Fails when |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `database` | `app/Health/DatabaseReady.php` | the default connection cannot be opened (down, refusing the login, or a lost SQLite file) |
| `cache` | `app/Health/CacheReady.php` | the default cache store cannot write a value and read it back |
| `scheduler` | `app/Health/SchedulerHeartbeat.php` | the scheduler heartbeat is missing or stale (below) |

Any failure answers 503 with the check names and statuses only; the reason goes to the log as `helmet.readiness_check_failed`. Point a readiness probe or a balancer at `/ready` and anything that restarts the app at `/up`. A hung database holds the probe for as long as the connection's own connect timeout, so on MySQL set `PDO::ATTR_TIMEOUT` in the connection's `options`. `tests/Feature/ReadyChecksTest.php` breaks the database and the cache in turn and expects 503.

### A stopped scheduler shows up[#](https://sourdough.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/laravel.html#a-stopped-scheduler-shows-up)

Citadel has no queue worker, so a generated app runs its queue from the scheduler (`QUEUE_WORKER_MODE=scheduler` starts a short `queue:work` each minute). A scheduler that stops does not error: it simply stops running, and jobs pile up in silence. Every Laravel shape therefore stamps a heartbeat into the cache each minute (`routes/console.php`, under the name `scheduler-heartbeat`), and `/ready` carries a `scheduler` check. While the stamp is missing or older than `WORKER_HEARTBEAT_MAX_AGE` seconds (default 180, `config/worker.php`), `/ready` answers 503, so a balancer or health probe skips the instance instead of feeding it work nobody will run. `/up` stays the liveness answer: it never looks at the cache, so a stalled scheduler does not take the app out of rotation for requests that do not need the queue.

### Every queued job has limits[#](https://sourdough.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/laravel.html#every-queued-job-has-limits)

A queued job with no limits retries as often as the worker allows and can hold a worker until the platform kills it. Every class under `app/Jobs` that implements `ShouldQueue` declares Laravel's `#[Tries]` and `#[Timeout]` attributes (on the class, a parent or a trait; the older `$tries` and `$timeout` properties count too), and the timeout stays below the queue connection's `retry_after` (Laravel's default is 90 seconds), or a second worker picks the job up while the first is still running it. `tests/Feature/JobLimitsTest.php` fails the suite on a job that breaks either rule, and passes while there are no jobs. The app ships `stubs/job.queued.stub` and `stubs/job.batched.queued.stub`, so `php artisan make:job` writes `#[Tries(3)]` and `#[Timeout(45)]` from the first job on.

### Work on the shared MySQL 5.6[#](https://sourdough.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/laravel.html#work-on-the-shared-mysql-5-6)

Laravel's database docs list MySQL 5.7+ and MariaDB 10.3+ as supported; the shared server is MySQL 5.6, which left extended support on 2021-02-28. The practical limit is the index key prefix: 767 bytes for REDUNDANT and COMPACT tables, which is 191 characters in utf8mb4. Laravel's default string column is 255 characters, so a unique index on it can fail with error 1071. The Laravel templates set the 191 default with `Schema::defaultStringLength(191)` in `app/Providers/AppServiceProvider.php` and avoid JSON columns, so string columns stay inside the limit (PROCTOR `mysql56-string-default`). Sail's MySQL is current, so a developer's migrations can pass locally and fail on deploy.

### Next steps[#](https://sourdough.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/laravel.html#next-steps)

Each Laravel bake prints Next steps suited to the shape. For `--laravel`:

```bash
composer install
cp .env.example .env
php artisan key:generate
php artisan migrate
php artisan serve
```

The islands and Inertia shapes add the front-end build between `migrate` and `serve`:

```bash
npm install
npm run build
```

The bake runs `php artisan migrate` after `php artisan key:generate`, so a freshly baked app has its database before the first request instead of answering 500 until someone migrates by hand.

### The Oracle check[#](https://sourdough.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/laravel.html#the-oracle-check)

Oracle is wired but dormant in every generated app. The settings `ORACLE_USERNAME`, `ORACLE_PASSWORD`, and either `ORACLE_TNS` or `ORACLE_HOST`, `ORACLE_PORT`, `ORACLE_SERVICE_NAME` ship commented out in `.env.example`; while they are empty, nothing connects and nothing errors. Once you fill them in, Laravel apps check the wiring with:

```bash
php artisan oracle:check
```

The command finds the check file where it lives: `oracle-check.php` at the app root, where Squire's Laravel layout ships it, first, then `deploy/oracle-check.php`.

## The manifest[#](https://sourdough.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/manifest.html#the-manifest)

Every app Sourdough generates carries a `.sourdough/manifest.json`, the starter's memory of what went into the loaf. This page explains what it records and how to check your app against it; commit the manifest so `sourdough feed` can bring template updates in without clobbering what you have changed.

### What it records[#](https://sourdough.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/manifest.html#what-it-records)

The manifest records the Sourdough version, the template, the answers you chose, and a sha256 hash of every file. Its keys, sorted alphabetically in the JSON:

| Key | Value |
| --- | --- |
| `answers` | each option you chose, sorted by key: the name, the shape flags, `sail` or `docker`, and the Playbook and ADVISOR choices |
| `files` | every generated file with its `sha256` hash and a `class` of `managed` or `seeded`, including the `--sail` and `--docker` files |
| `generated_at` | the generation time (or, after a feed, the time of the new bake), UTC |
| `schema` | the manifest schema version, currently `1` |
| `sourdough_version` | the Sourdough package version, or `dev` when it cannot be determined (running from a git checkout without a release tag) |
| `template` | the template the app was generated from |

The JSON is pretty-printed with sorted keys and a trailing newline, and paths use forward slashes on every OS, so two runs with the same answers differ only in `generated_at`.

### Managed and seeded[#](https://sourdough.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/manifest.html#managed-and-seeded)

| Class | Who owns it |
| --- | --- |
| `managed` | Sourdough owns the file and will update it |
| `seeded` | Sourdough wrote the file once; you own it now (`.env.example`, `README.md`, and `package-lock.json` on the shapes with a front end) |

The manifest remembers what went into the loaf, so `feed` knows what to refresh and what to leave to rise on its own. `sourdough feed` reads it to bring template updates into your app without clobbering what you've changed: see [Keeping apps current](https://sourdough.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/keeping-current.html).

### After a feed[#](https://sourdough.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/manifest.html#after-a-feed)

`sourdough feed` moves the manifest to the new base: the hashes of the loaf the installed Sourdough bakes today, and its version. Next to the manifest it keeps `.sourdough/base/`, one `<file>.base` per managed file you have changed, holding the template's version of that file. That is the base the next feed merges from, even when git history no longer has it. The `.base` suffix keeps a kept `.gitignore` from ignoring anything and keeps linters out. Commit the folder with the manifest, and do not edit it either.

### Check an app against its manifest[#](https://sourdough.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/manifest.html#check-an-app-against-its-manifest)

`sourdough manifest --check` lists the managed files that have drifted from the manifest, the files a feed will merge rather than replace:

```bash
sourdough manifest --check
```

You can pass the app directory as an argument; the default is the current directory. The exit codes match PROCTOR:

- `0` clean: `Clean: every managed file matches the manifest.`
- `1` a managed file changed or is missing: one line per file, `changed <file>` or `missing <file>`
- `2` tool error: no manifest in the directory, or no `--check`

Seeded files are never reported. They're yours. Line endings are forgiven, as `feed` forgives them: a file a checkout turned to CRLF still matches the LF bytes Sourdough wrote. Every shape's pipeline runs the check in its `sourdough-feed` job and lists what drifted without failing on it: see [Feed in CI](https://sourdough.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/keeping-current.html#feed-in-ci).

Tip

Commit `.sourdough/manifest.json` in your app. It's the record that keeps `feed` honest.

### The saved plan is not in the manifest[#](https://sourdough.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/manifest.html#the-saved-plan-is-not-in-the-manifest)

`.sourdough/plan.yaml`, the plan the app was baked from, sits next to the manifest but is not listed in it, so it is neither managed nor seeded. The manifest lists what the template wrote; the plan is what you asked for. `sourdough manifest --check` never reports it and `sourdough feed` never touches it, so edit it as the app grows and commit it with the manifest. See [The saved plan](https://sourdough.apps.wayne.edu/docs/reference/plan-format.html#the-saved-plan).

### The Squire deploy files[#](https://sourdough.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/manifest.html#the-squire-deploy-files)

The deploy files in your app (`build.sh`, `scripts/release.sh`, the `.squire/` config, and their friends) come from Squire's exported copy, checked into this repository at `templates/squire/`. Squire owns them; Sourdough installs them as-is and records them in the manifest, so you never edit them by hand. To refresh them, run `composer squire-copy:sync`, which rewrites the copy from the installed `waynestate/squire` package, then verify it with `composer squire-copy:check` (part of `composer ci`).

## Quick start[#](https://sourdough.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/quick-start.html#quick-start)

From a machine where `sourdough` is installed (see [Install](https://sourdough.apps.wayne.edu/docs/install.html)), bake an app and prove it.

### Steps[#](https://sourdough.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/quick-start.html#steps)

1. Scaffold the app.
   ```
   sourdough new my-app
   ```
   Expected: exit code `0` (done). The `my-app` directory appears with a Wayne State app in it: SESAME (auth), HELMET (baseline runtime), PROCTOR (checks), and the Preflight CI components already wired in. Sourdough prints Next steps for the new app.
2. Run the app's own checks.
   From inside `my-app/`:
   ```
   composer ci
   ```
   Expected: exit code `0`. A freshly baked app passes its own `composer ci` on the first run.

### What you built[#](https://sourdough.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/quick-start.html#what-you-built)

- A Wayne State app with the stack already wired in: SESAME (auth), HELMET (baseline runtime), PROCTOR (checks), and the Preflight CI components.
- Playbook wiring by default: the VCS repository, the package in `require`, `config.gitlab-domains` so Composer sends your token to git.wayne.edu, the seven setting names in `.env.example`, a `composer playbook` script that shows whether Playbook is installed, and a "WSU values (PLAYBOOK)" README section.
- ADVISOR in `require-dev`, a git-ignored `.mcp.json`, and an "ADVISOR" README section.
- `.sourdough/manifest.json`, the starter's memory: the Sourdough version, the template, the answers you chose, and a sha256 hash of every file, each marked `managed` (Sourdough owns it and will update it) or `seeded` (Sourdough wrote it once and you own it now: `.env.example`, `README.md`, and `package-lock.json` on the shapes with a front end).
- `.sourdough/plan.yaml`, the plan the app was baked from: the shape, the name and the stack parts (plus the models and pages, when you baked from a plan file). It bakes the same loaf again with `--plan`; see [The saved plan](https://sourdough.apps.wayne.edu/docs/reference/plan-format.html#the-saved-plan).

### Next steps[#](https://sourdough.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/quick-start.html#next-steps)

- Follow the app's printed Next steps: they point at `composer playbook` once dependencies are in, and at `php vendor/bin/advisor install --client=claude --write` for ADVISOR.
- [Pick a shape](https://sourdough.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/shapes.html): the permutations, from raw PHP to Laravel plus Inertia/Vue.
- [Describe a plan](https://sourdough.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/describe-a-plan.html): describe what the app does and let a model plan it.
- [The manifest](https://sourdough.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/manifest.html): what the manifest records, and `sourdough manifest --check`.
- [CI](https://sourdough.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/ci.html): set up the generated app's CI; a git.wayne.edu instance runner is strongly recommended.
- [Commands](https://sourdough.apps.wayne.edu/docs/reference/commands.html): every flag and option.

---

Source: https://sourdough.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/shapes.html

## Pick a shape[#](https://sourdough.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/shapes.html#pick-a-shape)

A starter in a jar is only potential until you give it a shape: pick the permutation below, then run `sourdough new` with the matching flags. If you would rather describe the app in a sentence and let a model plan it, continue to [Describe a plan](https://sourdough.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/describe-a-plan.html).

![Five loaves on the proofing bench (raw, raw + vue, blade, blade + islands, inertia) above the feeding schedule chalkboard](https://sourdough.apps.wayne.edu/docs/readme/gallery.jpg)

### The five permutations[#](https://sourdough.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/shapes.html#the-five-permutations)

| Flags | Permutation |
| --- | --- |
| (none) or `--raw` | Raw PHP with WayneUI's standalone path |
| `--raw --vue` | Raw PHP + Vue SPA over JSON |
| `--laravel` | Laravel + Blade |
| `--laravel --vue` | Laravel + Blade + Vue islands |
| `--laravel --inertia` (or `--inertia`) | Laravel + Inertia/Vue |

All five permutations bake: raw PHP since 0.1.0, the three Laravel shapes since 0.1.5 and raw PHP + Vue since 0.1.6. `--raw --vue` is the raw PHP bake with a Vue 3 front end over it: PHP answers JSON under `/api/`, Vite builds the Vue app, and `src/Vite.php` loads it from the build or the dev server.

Run `sourdough new` with the flags for the row you want. `dir` is the directory to create the app in:

raw

```bash
sourdough new my-app --raw
```

raw + vue

```bash
sourdough new my-app --raw --vue
```

laravel

```bash
sourdough new my-app --laravel
```

laravel + vue

```bash
sourdough new my-app --laravel --vue
```

inertia

```bash
sourdough new my-app --inertia
```

### The template directories[#](https://sourdough.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/shapes.html#the-template-directories)

Each shape bakes from a directory in `templates/`:

| Template directory | Shape |
| --- | --- |
| `raw/` | Raw PHP with WayneUI's standalone path |
| `raw-vue/` | Raw PHP + Vue SPA over JSON (copied over `raw/`) |
| `laravel-blade/` | Laravel + Blade |
| `laravel-blade-vue/` | Laravel + Blade + Vue islands |
| `laravel-inertia/` | Laravel + Inertia/Vue |

`squire/` holds Squire's exported deploy files. Squire owns them; Sourdough installs them as-is into every app and records them in the manifest, so you never edit them by hand.

The raw template also carries its own checks:

- Pinstripe's coding standard: `pint.json` (the per preset, with the fetched `public/wayne-ui.php` kept out and `vendor` excluded) and `phpstan.neon` (Pinstripe's raw preset, level 8 over `src/` and `public/`), with `waynestate/pinstripe` in require-dev and the extension-installer plugin allowed, and `lint`, `fix` and `analyse` scripts, so `composer ci` runs test, lint, analyse, proctor and audit in that order.
- An explicit `composer-ci` job in `.gitlab-ci.yml` (`composer install`, then `composer ci`), mirroring the Laravel overlay, so PROCTOR sees a `composer ci` in the pipeline instead of warning that no job runs it.
- `stubs/wayne-ui.php`, a static-analysis stub for the run-time WayneUI functions (`wsu_shell_start`, `wsu_shell_end`) that `phpstan.neon` scans through `scanFiles`.
- A front controller that answers `404` for any path but `/` (a short not-found page that keeps WayneUI's layout and links home) instead of rendering the home page for every URL; `/up` stays HELMET's and answers first.

### Raw PHP + Vue[#](https://sourdough.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/shapes.html#raw-php-vue)

`--raw --vue` keeps everything above and swaps the page for a Vue 3 app. PHP boots HELMET, the session and SESAME the same way, then answers JSON under `/api/` (`/api/me` is the signed-in user) and sends one page that loads the Vue app. WayneUI comes from its Vue package and its layered dist stylesheet, pinned as in the Inertia shape, so there is no `public/wayne-ui.php` to fetch. Run it with:

```bash
composer install
npm install
npm run build
composer serve
```

Run `npm run dev` in a second terminal for hot reload: `src/Vite.php` loads the app from the dev server while it runs, and from `public/build` otherwise. See [Templates](https://sourdough.apps.wayne.edu/docs/reference/templates.html#raw-vue) for every file it adds.

### Oracle in every shape[#](https://sourdough.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/shapes.html#oracle-in-every-shape)

Oracle is wired but dormant in every generated app. The settings `ORACLE_USERNAME`, `ORACLE_PASSWORD`, and either `ORACLE_TNS` or `ORACLE_HOST`, `ORACLE_PORT`, `ORACLE_SERVICE_NAME` ship commented out in `.env.example`; while they are empty, nothing connects and nothing errors. Once you fill them in, Laravel apps check the wiring with `php artisan oracle:check`, and raw PHP apps run queries through the `App\Oracle` helper, which takes values only as binds and answers mistakes with plain sentences. The command finds the check file where it lives: `oracle-check.php` at the app root, where Squire's Laravel layout ships it, first, then `deploy/oracle-check.php`.

### Related[#](https://sourdough.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/shapes.html#related)

- [Describe a plan](https://sourdough.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/describe-a-plan.html)
- [The manifest](https://sourdough.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/manifest.html)

Source: https://sourdough.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/support.html

## Support and sunset[#](https://sourdough.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/support.html#support-and-sunset)

Starters die quietly when nobody owns them. This page is the policy for Sourdough's five shapes: who owns each one, how long it is supported, and how one is retired without surprising the apps baked from it. Even the best loaf goes stale; the point is to say so before it does.

The facts behind the policy are data, not prose: `resources/shapes.json` holds each shape's owner, status and sunset fields, and `sourdough new --dry-run --json` reports them with the dates the app inherits from CREED.

### Owners[#](https://sourdough.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/support.html#owners)

Every shape names an owner role, never a person. Today all five belong to the same role:

| Shape | Owner | Status |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `raw` | Sourdough maintainers | supported |
| `raw-vue` | Sourdough maintainers | supported |
| `laravel-blade` | Sourdough maintainers | supported |
| `laravel-blade-vue` | Sourdough maintainers | supported |
| `laravel-inertia` | Sourdough maintainers | supported |

The Sourdough maintainers are the role that releases Sourdough (Enterprise Applications). The owner keeps the shape green in the smoke and proof jobs, answers its issues, and decides when it is deprecated. A change to the Inertia shape also lands in WELD, which is generated from it, in the same round of work.

### How long a shape is supported[#](https://sourdough.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/support.html#how-long-a-shape-is-supported)

Note

The windows below are a proposal and are not confirmed yet. The rules for marking and announcing a deprecation are in force now.

- A shape is supported while `resources/shapes.json` lists it as `supported`. Only the newest Sourdough release gets fixes; an app stays supported by feeding (`sourdough feed`), which its own `sourdough-feed` CI job reminds it to do.
- The app inherits its framework's clock. The Laravel shapes generate the newest Laravel major, and CREED's policy holds that major's end of security support (`sourdough new` prints it; for Laravel 13 it is 2028-03-17). Proposal: Sourdough moves the Laravel shapes to a new major within 90 days of its release, so a fed app is never stuck on a major that is about to end.
- The raw shapes follow PHP alone: their floor comes from CREED (see [The PHP floor](https://sourdough.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/support.html#the-php-floor)), and `sourdough new` prints that line's end of security support.
- Proposal: a shape is supported for as long as its framework line has a supported successor that the shape can move to. When it has none, or no one in the owner role can keep it green, it is deprecated as below.

### How a shape is retired[#](https://sourdough.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/support.html#how-a-shape-is-retired)

A retirement is announced one release ahead, the same way Preflight retires a component (see [Preflight: deprecating a component](https://preflight.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/deprecation.html)):

1. **Deprecate.** In a release, the shape's entry in `resources/shapes.json` changes to `"status": "deprecated"` with `deprecated_in` (this release), `removed_in` (a later release) and `replacement` (the shape to move to). The CHANGELOG gets a `Deprecated:` bullet naming the shape and its replacement, and the upgrading page says what to do.
2. **Say so on every run.** From that release, `sourdough new` prints `Deprecated: The <shape> shape is deprecated since Sourdough <x> and is removed in <y>; move to <shape>.` and `sourdough feed` adds the same line to its notes, so every pipeline's `sourdough-feed` job shows it. Nothing fails because of it.
3. **Keep it bakeable.** The shape keeps baking and feeding for at least one release, and (proposal) at least 6 months after the deprecation release.
4. **Remove.** In the `removed_in` release the generator goes, and the entry changes to `"status": "removed"`. Feeding an app of that shape stops with the same notice, naming the replacement. Published tags are never moved, so an older Sourdough release still bakes the old shape for anyone who needs it.

`tests/ShapeSupportTest.php` holds the catalog to these rules: every shape Sourdough bakes is listed with an owner; a supported shape carries no sunset fields; a deprecated or removed shape names the release that deprecated it, a later release that removes it, and a replacement Sourdough still bakes; and a removed shape is one Sourdough no longer bakes.

### The fields[#](https://sourdough.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/support.html#the-fields)

`resources/shapes.json`, one entry per shape:

| Field | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `owner` | the owner role (never a person) |
| `status` | `supported`, `deprecated` or `removed` |
| `deprecated_in` | the Sourdough release that deprecated the shape, or `null` |
| `removed_in` | the release that removes it (later than `deprecated_in`), or `null` |
| `replacement` | the shape to move to, or `null` |

`sourdough new <dir> --dry-run --json` adds two objects to the plan:

- `support`: the shape's entry plus `policy` (this page) and `runs_on`, the line the app inherits its clock from (`{"component": "laravel", "version": "13", "security_until": "2028-03-17"}` for a Laravel shape, the PHP floor line for a raw one).
- `php`: the floor the bake writes (`constraint`, `platform`, `versions`), the floor line's `floor_security_until`, and where it came from (`source`, `origin`, `refreshed_on`, `horizon_days`, and `reason` when the fallback was used).

### The PHP floor[#](https://sourdough.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/support.html#the-php-floor)

A new app's PHP floor is not a number in a template: Sourdough reads it from CREED's `policy.json` when it bakes, the same file PROCTOR's `php-floor` check reads in the app.

- **Source.** The policy installed with `waynestate/creed` (a Sourdough dependency), or the file the `SOURDOUGH_POLICY` environment variable names.
- **The rule.** As of the policy's own `refreshed_on` date, look 365 days ahead; the floor is the oldest PHP line CREED's reader still calls supported on that later date. A new app never starts on a line that ends inside its first year. The Laravel shapes raise it to the Laravel major's minimum PHP when that is higher. The policy's date is used, not today's clock, so the same Sourdough and the same policy always bake the same loaf, and the floor moves only when the policy does.
- **What it writes.** `require.php` (`^8.3`) and `config.platform.php` (`8.3.0`) in `composer.json`; the `php_versions` matrix in `.gitlab-ci.yml` (every line from the floor up that is supported and has a Docker image in the policy, capped at the Laravel major's maximum PHP); the comment above it; and the README's test-suite line.
- **Fallback.** When the policy cannot be read or does not answer, the bake still works on the pinned values the templates carry (`^8.3`, tested on 8.3, 8.4 and 8.5) and says `pinned fallback` with the reason. A test fails when the policy and the fallback disagree, so the pin is moved with the policy.
- **Moving an app.** When CREED moves the floor, the next Sourdough release bakes the new one, and `sourdough feed` brings it into apps already baked, merged like any template change.

Note

The 365-day horizon is a proposal. CREED is the natural owner of it; until CREED's policy carries one, the number lives in `src/PhpFloor.php`.

- [Upgrading](https://sourdough.apps.wayne.edu/docs/upgrading.html)

## Testing[#](https://sourdough.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/testing.html#testing)

This page is the proofing bench: how to run Sourdough's own checks day to day, and how to fire the smoke gate that bakes a shape for real before it may be claimed. Like any starter, Sourdough needs regular feeding, or it goes flat. For the wider runbook, continue to [Maintaining](https://sourdough.apps.wayne.edu/docs/maintaining.html).

Note

Maintainers: how to build, test and release this project, and where its data comes from, is in [MAINTAINING.md](https://sourdough.apps.wayne.edu/docs/maintaining.html).

### Day-to-day commands[#](https://sourdough.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/testing.html#day-to-day-commands)

| Task | Command |
| --- | --- |
| Install | `composer install` |
| All checks (what CI runs) | `composer ci` |
| Only the tests | `composer test` |
| Fix code style | `composer fix` |
| Check the Squire copy | `composer squire-copy:check` |
| Refresh the Squire copy | `composer squire-copy:sync`, then commit `templates/squire/` |
| Try a generation | `php bin/sourdough new ./demo --raw --dry-run` |

`composer ci` runs `composer validate --strict`, the tests, Pint, PHPStan, the Squire copy check, the agent-ready files check, the docs site check and `composer audit`. The tests fail on any PHP or PHPUnit deprecation (`failOnDeprecation` and `failOnPhpunitDeprecation` in `phpunit.xml.dist`), and the report names the test that raised it, the same gate every baked app gets.

### With only Docker[#](https://sourdough.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/testing.html#with-only-docker)

The same lines work in PowerShell and sh:

```
docker run --rm -v "${PWD}:/app" -v stack-composer-cache:/tmp/cache -w /app composer:2.10.3 sh -c "composer install --no-interaction && composer ci"
docker run --rm -v "${PWD}:/app" -w /app php:8.5-cli vendor/bin/phpunit
```

The `stack-composer-cache` volume keeps Composer's downloads between runs; Docker creates it the first time.

### From the repo root[#](https://sourdough.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/testing.html#from-the-repo-root)

```
docker run --rm -v "${PWD}:/app" -v stack-composer-cache:/tmp/cache -w /app composer:2 composer install --no-interaction
docker run --rm -v "${PWD}:/app" -w /app php:8.3-cli vendor/bin/phpunit
docker run --rm -v "${PWD}:/app" -w /app php:8.4-cli vendor/bin/phpunit
docker run --rm -v "${PWD}:/app" -v stack-composer-cache:/tmp/cache -w /app composer:2 composer validate --strict
docker run --rm -v "${PWD}:/app" -w /app php:8.4-cli php bin/sourdough new /tmp/demo --dry-run
```

### The smoke gate[#](https://sourdough.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/testing.html#the-smoke-gate)

The smoke gate is the proofing bench: it proofs one shape at a time before that shape may be claimed. It bakes the app with this checkout's own `bin/sourdough new <dir> --no-advisor --no-playbook --no-input` (the CLI under test is the one being shipped). Every bake passes `--no-playbook`, because Playbook is the default wiring but its package is private on git.wayne.edu and the gate must run credential-free.

Right after the bake, every shape proves its manifest and its bake: `sourdough manifest --check` must be clean, and with the fresh app committed to a scratch git repository `sourdough feed --dry-run` must find nothing to feed (a bake that is not stable would make every feed of it a conflict). The repository is dropped again before the app's own checks:

- `raw`: `composer install`, `composer test`, `composer proctor` and `composer ci`, then a live check: fetch the pinned WayneUI release once into `public/wayne-ui.php`, start the app with `APP_ENV=local` and expect `/` 200 with the app's home page in WayneUI's shell, `/nope` 404 and `/up` 200 (the front controller defaults `APP_ENV` to production when it is unset, so the server must set it)
- `raw-vue`: the raw steps plus `npm ci --ignore-scripts` (from the shipped `package-lock.json`) and `npm run build`, then the same live server, which must answer `/` with the built app mounted on `id="app"`, `/api/me` with the signed-in user (and `401` without a session), `/nope` with `404` and the app, and `/up` with `200`
- `blade`: `composer install`, `cp .env.example .env`, `php artisan key:generate`, `php artisan migrate`, `php artisan test`, `composer proctor` and `composer ci`, then Laravel's own router (the one `php artisan serve` runs) must answer `/` with the Blade home page, `/dashboard` after SESAME's fake sign-in, `/nope` with `404` and `/up` with `200`
- `blade-vue`: the blade steps with `npm ci --ignore-scripts` and `npm run build` before the tests; `/` must also load the built assets and `/dashboard` carry the Vue island
- `inertia`: the blade-vue steps plus `npm run typecheck`; `/` must hand Vue the Inertia `Home` page and `/dashboard` the `Dashboard` page

With `--sail` or `--docker` after the shape (`smoke-shape.sh blade --docker`), a Laravel shape proves its oven instead: the scaffold's files are there, then `composer install`, `php artisan key:generate`, `php artisan test` and `composer proctor`. The gate never lights the oven: it has no Docker daemon.

With `SMOKE_FEED_FROM` set to a release (for example `0.1.6`), the gate also bakes the shape with that release from Packagist, commits it, and feeds it forward with this checkout: no conflict, a clean manifest afterwards, nothing left to feed. `scripts/proof.sh` (`scripts/proof.ps1` on Windows) runs every shape and every oven this way, one after another, and writes the Last run table on the [Proof](https://sourdough.apps.wayne.edu/docs/reference/proof.html) page.

Each step prints `ok`; the first `FAIL` stops the run and shows the command's tail. A shape is claimed in the docs only when its smoke is green.

`tests/FeedCommandTest.php` covers `sourdough feed` itself on every shape (and with `--sail` and `--docker`), offline, in the PHPUnit suite: an app aged to an older template, one with local edits that merge cleanly, one with a conflict, a file that already has the template's new version, an oven app baked by 0.1.6, and the refusals. It needs git on PATH and skips without it.

Run it per OS. The image (`scripts/smoke.Dockerfile`) pins php 8.5, composer 2 and node 22, so the bake is identical everywhere:

linux

```bash
docker build -f scripts/smoke.Dockerfile -t sourdough-smoke:local .
docker run --rm -v "$PWD:/repo:ro" -v /work -e SMOKE_WORK=/work sourdough-smoke:local sh /repo/scripts/smoke-shape.sh <shape>
```

windows

```powershell
.\scripts\smoke-shape.ps1 <shape>
```

The PowerShell wrapper builds the same image once and reuses it. Pass `-WorkDir <dir>` to bind a local folder to `/work` so the scratch copy, the generated app and the per-step logs survive the run, `-Oven sail` or `-Oven docker` for an oven run, and `-FeedFrom <version>` to feed a release forward. On Windows, `.\scripts\smoke-shape.ps1 <shape>` runs it in one line.

Environment variables:

- `SMOKE_WORK`: the scratch dir for the copy, the app and the logs. Defaults to a fresh temp dir that is removed on exit.
- `SMOKE_KEEP`: set to `1` to keep the scratch dir behind for inspection.
- `SMOKE_FEED_FROM`: a released Sourdough to bake and feed forward (off when unset).
- `SMOKE_PREV_CACHE`: where that release is installed, so several runs share one copy.
- `SMOKE_PORT`: the live server's port (default `8099`).

### Proof the lot[#](https://sourdough.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/testing.html#proof-the-lot)

`sh scripts/proof.sh` (Linux, macOS) and `.\scripts\proof.ps1` (Windows) run the gate on all eleven runs (five shapes, six ovens), feed the last release forward in each, and write the Last run table. What each run proves and the latest results are on the [Proof](https://sourdough.apps.wayne.edu/docs/reference/proof.html) page.

Note

On CI the gate runs as one job per shape: `smoke` (matrix) on GitHub, `smoke-raw`, `smoke-raw-vue`, `smoke-blade`, `smoke-blade-vue` and `smoke-inertia` on GitLab. All are `allow_failure: true` until the lead has seen every shape green on CI once; flip them to blocking after that proof. The whole proof runs in the GitLab `proof` job, by hand or on a schedule that sets `SOURDOUGH_PROOF` to `1`, never on a push.
